content: In mathematics, the concept of dimension is defined as the minimum number of coordinates required to specify any point within a given space. Dimensions can be visualized as axes in a Cartesian coordinate system. For example, in a three-dimensional system, the axes represent left-right, up-down, and forward-backward directions. A point in this space can be uniquely identified using three coordinates corresponding to these axes. In the physical world, according to the theory of relativity, time is considered the fourth dimension, which progresses in a before-after direction. Thus, an event's position in space and time is fully described by four coordinates. On two-dimensional surfaces, such as a plane or the surface of a sphere, only two numbers are needed to specify a point, making these spaces two-dimensional. Similarly, a line is one-dimensional because only one coordinate is required, while a point has no dimensions. In mathematics, spaces with more than three dimensions are used to describe other types of manifolds. In these n-dimensional spaces, a point is located using n coordinates, denoted as (x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ). Some mathematical theories, such as those in fractal geometry, utilize non-integer and even negative dimensions. In physics, the term dimension also refers to the nature of measurable quantities. For instance, physical measurements that require units, such as length (L), time (T), or speed (L/T), are considered dimensionful. Speed, defined as the distance traveled per unit of time, has the dimension L T⁻¹, while acceleration, the change in speed per unit of time, has the dimension L T⁻². In mathematics, no single definition of dimension is universally applicable across all contexts. Consequently, mathematicians have developed various definitions tailored to different types of spaces. These definitions are often based on the concept of Euclidean n-space (Eⁿ). For example, a point (E⁰) is zero-dimensional, a line (E¹) is one-dimensional, and a plane (E²) is two-dimensional. In general, Eⁿ is n-dimensional. A tesseract serves as an example of a four-dimensional object. While non-mathematicians might say, A tesseract has four dimensions, mathematicians would express this as The tesseract has dimension 4. Historically, the idea of higher dimensions in mathematics was introduced by Bernhard Riemann in 1854. He abstractly considered a point as a set of n numbers (x₁, ..., xₙ) without requiring a geometric representation. For vector spaces, the dimension is defined as the cardinality of a basis, known as the Hamel dimension. In the context of topological manifolds, the dimension is determined by the number n such that the manifold is locally homeomorphic to Euclidean n-space. This yields a uniquely defined dimension for every connected topological manifold. The study of manifolds reveals that dimensions 1 and 2 are relatively simple, higher dimensions (n > 4) are easier to work with due to additional space, and dimensions 3 and 4 are the most challenging. This complexity is evident in the Poincaré conjecture, which required different proof methods for various dimensions. The Lebesgue covering dimension of a topological space X is defined as the smallest integer n such that any open cover of X has an open refinement where no point is included in more than n+1 elements. If no such integer exists, the dimension of X is considered infinite. This definition can be extended to Tychonoff spaces by replacing open with functionally open. The inductive dimension of a topological space is based on the analogy that n+1-dimensional balls have n-dimensional boundaries, allowing for an inductive definition based on the dimensions of the boundaries of open sets. For sets with complex structures, such as fractals, the Hausdorff dimension is particularly useful. It is defined for all metric spaces and can take non-integer real values, unlike the Hamel dimension. Variants like the box dimension or Minkowski dimension are also used. These definitions are especially relevant for highly irregular sets and can yield non-integer positive real values. In Hilbert spaces, the dimension is determined by the cardinality of an orthonormal basis, which is the same for any two such bases in a given space. This dimension is finite if and only if the space's Hamel dimension is finite, in which case the two dimensions coincide. The Krull dimension of a commutative ring is defined as the maximal number of strict inclusions in an increasing chain of prime ideals within the ring. This concept is named after Wolfgang Krull. Negative dimensions, introduced by Benoit Mandelbrot, extend the concept of fractal dimensions. When positive, they align with known definitions, but when negative, they measure the emptiness of empty sets. In classical physics, three spatial dimensions are described as up/down, left/right, and forward/backward. Movement in any other direction can be expressed as a combination of these three. A line represents one dimension, a plane represents two dimensions, and a cube represents three dimensions. Time is often referred to as the fourth dimension and is a measure of physical change. Unlike spatial dimensions, time progresses at a fixed rate of one second per second, and we cannot move freely through it. The perception of time flowing in one direction is an artifact of the laws of thermodynamics, specifically the increase in entropy. The best-known treatment of time as a dimension is found in Einstein's theory of relativity, which combines space and time into a four-dimensional manifold called spacetime. Theories like string theory and M-theory propose that physical space has additional dimensions, with 10 and 11 dimensions, respectively. These extra dimensions are thought to be curled up at subatomic scales, possibly at the level of quarks or strings. However, no physical experiments have confirmed the existence of these additional dimensions. Sir Roger Penrose's singularity theorem suggests that theories attributing more than three spatial dimensions and one temporal dimension to the physical world are unstable. Such systems would rapidly collapse into a singularity, making the unification of gravity with other forces through extra dimensions impossible. In the physical sciences and engineering, the dimension of a physical quantity expresses the class of physical unit against which it is measured. For example, the dimension of speed is L T⁻¹, representing length divided by time. The units used, such as meters per second (m/s) or miles per hour (mph), must conform to this dimension. In science fiction, the term dimension is often used to refer to parallel universes, alternate realities, or other planes of existence. This usage stems from the idea that traveling to such realms requires movement in a spatial direction beyond the standard three. One of the most celebrated works exploring true geometric dimensionality is the 1884 novella Flatland by Edwin A. Abbott, which serves as an excellent introduction to the concept of dimensions.
